sections: Keep the familiar cities, then widen the comparison

Hyderabad, Lucknow and Kolkata are useful starting points, but they do not describe all of India's biryani traditions. Keep this page as a way to ask better questions at the table rather than a recipe rule that every kitchen must follow. Tamil Nadu offers additional named styles worth looking for, especially when you are already travelling in the state.
Ask what is in this kitchen's version

Before ordering, ask which meat or vegetables are used, what rice the kitchen cooks with and how much is in a portion. A city label does not answer an allergy question or promise the same level of spice everywhere. Ask whether accompaniments are included and whether a bone-in serving is intended for one person or sharing.
Ambur: a Tamil Nadu lead

Tamil Nadu Tourism identifies Ambur biryani with seeraga samba rice and describes coriander, mint and curd among its flavour elements. Treat that as regional background, not a complete ingredient declaration for a restaurant dish. Ask the kitchen about the meat, dairy and side dishes before ordering.
Dindigul: a different regional comparison

The same state tourism page identifies Dindigul biryani with jeera samba rice, pepper and green chilli, and describes a distinct tangy character. This adds a concrete subject beyond the three better-known city comparisons. It does not mean every restaurant using the Dindigul name follows one identical recipe. Ask what is being cooked that day and how it is served.
Chettinad and Rawther styles

Tamil Nadu Tourism also describes Chettinad biryani and Rawther biryani associated with Coimbatore and the Palakkad region. These are further regional leads, not a claim that their recipes are fixed or interchangeable. If you are exploring differences, try smaller portions on different days rather than ordering more food than you can enjoy at one meal.
Bhatkal: onion-rich rice and a separate vermicelli tradition

Bhatkal on the Karnataka coast has a Navayath food tradition worth seeking on its own terms. Independent reporting describes basmati rice with an onion-heavy masala and chicken, mutton or prawns; shaiyyo biryani uses vermicelli instead. These are useful questions for a local kitchen, not interchangeable names for one dish. Do not assume that a serving is oil-free: an account of rice cooked without added fat also describes oil used in the masala.
Bohri biryani: ask about the meal around the rice

Bohra food is a community cuisine, not a promise of one fixed restaurant recipe. Reporting on Mumbai's food scene describes chicken seekh dum biryani and rice courses within a thaal meal that alternates sweet and savoury dishes. Ask whether you are ordering a standalone biryani or joining a multi-course meal, what sharing arrangements are used, and what ingredients are in this kitchen's preparation. An old account of a pop-up does not confirm that the same event or menu runs today.
Guntur: an Andhra comparison, not another name for Hyderabad

Guntur belongs to Andhra Pradesh. Reporting on Andhra restaurants describes a red-chilli-led Guntur biryani and, in Hyderabad, a masala-rich Guntur-style option alongside other regional rice dishes. Ask about the actual chilli intensity before ordering rather than treating a regional label as a competition. The name does not establish a standard meat cut, rice variety or serving price across restaurants.
Moti pulao: understand the pearl reference

Food historian Rana Safvi describes moti pulao in Lucknow's culinary history, with small decorative pearls and later versions using meatballs or paneer. The distinction between pulao and biryani matters here; do not expect every menu to use the same name. Ask a specialist kitchen what its version contains and whether it needs advance ordering. Historical use of decorative metal leaf is background, not a promise about a present-day dish.
Use the comparison, then check the kitchen

This regional sampler is a starting point, not a national inventory or a restaurant availability list. Ask about dairy, nuts, eggs, meat, seafood and shared utensils where relevant. Keep the history of a dish separate from the ingredient checks you need for your own meal. A familiar name never substitutes for a current menu or a conversation with the cook.
